name: Salas controlled aliasing (arXiv 2503.20162): claimed 2^{n/2-eps} subset sum, flaw verification
description: Jesus Salas's 'Beyond Worst-Case Subset Sum: An Adaptive, Structure-Aware Solver with Sub-2^{n/2} Enumeration' gives a deterministic unique-subset-sums enumerator with runtime O*(U n^2) (U = number of distinct subset sums) and a 'Controlled Aliasing' trick claimed to give a worst-case O*(2^{n/2-eps}) bound. Section 7 of the paper defines aliasing by treating x1 as x0 in one half's enumeration and keeping one canonical subset per resulting sum; the proof of the speedup is deferred to a companion paper and not given. The repo's NEXT.md counterexample is confirmed against the text: the aliasing changes the stored partial sums, so the merge phase can output wrong answers and lose true solutions. Do not cite the 2^{n/2-eps} claim.
authors_year_venue: Jesus Salas (independent researcher), arXiv 2503.20162v3 (cs.DS), 3 Dec 2025 version; companion theory paper cited as [9] (not read).
status_and_verification: Preprint, not peer reviewed. I read the abstract, introduction and Section 7 (Meet-in-the-Middle speed-up via Controlled Aliasing, lines ~985-1075 of the extracted text) in full, and skimmed the structure (Theorem 6 enumerator correctness, collision pruning). I did not read the companion paper, so the claimed proof of 2^{n/2-eps} is unevaluated rather than refuted; the counterexample refutes the described mechanism, not necessarily the existence of a different proof.
key_theorem_or_bound: Claim (abstract/Sec 7): with controlled aliasing, worst-case runtime O*(2^{n/2-eps}) for some constant eps>0; the formal analysis is in the companion paper: 'We do not reproduce that proof here.' The solver's proven bound: O*(U n^2) with U=|Sigma(S)|, never above O*(2^{n/2}). Mechanism: whenever a subset includes x1, its contribution is computed as x0; store lexicographically minimal subset per resulting sum.
regime_exponents: Claims to reduce the exponent n/2 by a constant eps for all inputs, including unstructured ones with near-maximal subset-sum diversity (U ~ 2^n); otherwise bound is min(U n^2, 2^{n/2}) type. Practical claim: injecting one duplicate per half and restricting to subsets of size <= n/4 per half reduces enumeration to below 40% of naive on average.
proof_type_and_tools: Combinatorial/algorithmic (enumeration with memoized collision detection, canonical representatives); the aliasing speedup rests on an unpublished 'combinatorial analysis of how injected duplicates collapse enumeration trees'.
quantitative_loss: Even if aliasing were sound, saving a constant number of aliased elements per half changes only a constant factor (e.g. factor 3/4 on a half), i.e. 2^{n/2} -> c 2^{n/2} with c<1, not a 2^{-eps n} exponent saving; claiming exponent reduction by constant eps requires aliasing Theta(n) elements, and then the false-positive/lost-solution damage grows. The paper itself says 'a small but nontrivial constant factor' in the abstract, which is not the same as exponent eps n.
worst_case_vs_average_case: Claims worst-case; the evidence offered in the main paper is empirical (collision-rich and random instances); no worst-case proof appears in the paper itself.
coefficient_set: {0,1} subset sums (also negative values/zero handled by remarks).
subset_size_regime: All subsets; the practical variant restricts to subsets of size <= n/4 per half (using complements for the rest).
relevance_to_Nc: None positive. It is a cautionary item: a sound solver exploiting collisions must handle the equal-sum structure without changing true sums. The correct role for collisions is exactly C1's: N_c counts pairs that already collide, not collisions forced by editing the input. The adaptive U-based enumerator (Section 5) is sound and shows runtime O*(U n^2), matching the idea that few distinct sums means easy.
relevance_to_Dstar: None directly; the U-parameterized runtime is the whole-set analogue of D* (distinct sums vs distinct balanced half-sums), but the paper gives no bound on U for hard instances.
applicability_gap: The aliasing step is not sound: replacing x1 by x0 changes the sum of any subset containing x1. In half {1,2}, aliasing 2 -> 1 gives subsets {1} and {2} both stored sum 1 and canonical subset {1,2} the stored sum 2 while its true sum is 3 (as in NEXT.md); the merge with the other half would therefore return a false positive and lose {2}, destroying completeness. A paper-stated 'correctness' hinge, 'a single canonical representation for each resulting sum', merges subsets with different true sums.
counterexample_or_hard_instance_family: Half {1,2}, aliasing 2->1: stored sums: {}:0, {1}:1, {2}:1, {1,2}:2; true sums 0,1,2,3. With the other half summing to the target t=3 (true solution {2} plus the other half sum 1, or {1,2} plus 0) the stored table cannot distinguish. This is a small counterexample of the form recorded in NEXT.md; I checked it by hand from the Section 7 description. Also hard instances for any sound solver: sets with 2^{Theta(n)} distinct sums (U ~ 2^n), such as dissociated sets.
dependency_chain: None sound. A sound adaptive solver would compose: (i) exact U-sensitive enumeration (Chan 2601.01390 / BFN output-sensitive), (ii) AKKN density dichotomy for the extreme bin sizes, (iii) a worst-case proof for the intermediate band (C1/C2 or Randolph-Wegrzycki representation).
constructiveness: The solver is constructive (returns subsets) but the speedup mechanism is unsound.
lean_formalizable: The counterexample (four partial sums, merge returns a wrong witness) is trivially formalizable and decidable; the correctness spec 'every stored partial sum equals the true sum of the stored subset' can be stated and shown violated by aliasing.
computational_check: Trivial: implement aliasing MITM for random n<=20 and compare to exact MITM; the paper's own experiments (not examined in detail) are empirical. In the repo, a brute-force check at n<=20 would exhibit lost solutions.
next_experiment: Implement the aliased MITM exactly as Section 7 describes and run it against exact MITM on random instances with n<=24; count false positives and missed solutions, to document the flaw empirically and attach it to the NEXT.md note.
open_issues: Companion paper [9] with the claimed 2^{n/2-eps} proof was not read; I cannot exclude that a different (sound) mechanism is intended there. What a sound adaptive solver would need: (a) an invariant that every stored sum is the true sum of the stored subset, (b) any collapse of states must be justified by true equal sums (e.g. identical sums of different subsets), not by modified weights, (c) a bound on how many states disappear in the worst case, which for inputs with 2^n distinct subset sums is zero, hence exponent savings cannot come from collapsing equal sums, so a 2^{n/2-eps} bound would have to come from some other source such as Chen-Jin-Randolph-Servedio's n^{0.5023} polynomial saving or a structure theorem (C1/C2). None of these is present in the source.
